title: Lambdas: code in a variable
summary: A functional interface has one method; a lambda is a short way to write it.

say.never: Some interfaces promise just **one** method. A greeter only has to greet. That kind is called a **functional interface**, and `@FunctionalInterface` on top asks Java to make sure it stays that way: add a second method and it won't compile.
say.bit: A **functional interface** has exactly one method. `@FunctionalInterface` makes Java check that.

steps.title: In your lesson: One job, one method

say.never: `SpeedFilter` has one job: take a speed and hand back a new speed. So it's a functional interface with one method, `apply`. Like any interface method, it ends in a semicolon with no body.
say.bit: `SpeedFilter` is a functional interface with one method: `double apply(double speed);`

say.never: Writing a whole class just to greet people politely is a lot of typing. A **lambda** does it in one line. Read `name -> "Hello, " + name` as "given a *name*, hand back Hello plus the name". The arrow `->` splits the input from the answer. Making the lambda doesn't run it. It runs each time you call `greet`.
say.bit: A **lambda**: `input -> answer`. It's a whole implementation of the one method, and it runs only when called.

say.never: Each method in `Filters` hands back a lambda instead of a number. `half()` returns a filter that, given a speed, hands back half of it. `invert()` is the same idea with the sign flipped.
say.bit: `half()` returns `speed -> speed * 0.5`. Write `invert()` the same way.

marks.label: a whole SpeedFilter in one line

say.never: When the answer needs an `if`, give the lambda a body in `{ }` and use `return`, like a small method. A lambda can also use the variables around it, like `maxLength` here: it remembers that value for later, even after `shortened` has finished.
say.bit: Need an `if`? Use `{ }` and `return`. A lambda can also use variables from around it.

marks.label: the lambda ends, then the return line does

say.never: `deadband(threshold)` returns a lambda with a body. If the speed is closer to zero than `threshold` (use `Math.abs(speed)` so small negative speeds count too), hand back `0.0`. Otherwise hand back the speed unchanged. That stops a robot creeping when the stick isn't quite centered.
say.bit: `deadband`: a `{ }` lambda that returns `0.0` when `Math.abs(speed) < threshold`, else `speed`.
